questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An exemption offset by charges on others
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a customs exemption actually covers
questions.stem: Ticket 214 asks the platform team to explain why a customs exemption granted for one shipment still left the merchant paying charges levied on other shipments.

options.text: The exemption applied only to the shipment it named, leaving charges on other shipments assessable.
The exemption covered every shipment in the account, so no further charge could be valid.
options.misconception: believes one exemption voids all other charges

options.text: The charges on other shipments were added later to punish the merchant for claiming the exemption.
options.misconception: assumes exemptions attract punitive surcharges

options.text: Other shipments needed a separate treaty before any exemption could be applied to them at all.
options.misconception: assumes a separate treaty is needed for other goods

questions.explanation: An exemption removes a duty for the specific good or shipment it names, not for everything else in the account. Every other shipment is assessed on its own entry, so its charges survive.
questions.hint: Ask what the exemption actually names.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A duty schedule fixed by treaty
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a treaty duty schedule settles and what it leaves open
questions.stem: Ticket 215 asks for a plain account of what a duty schedule fixed by treaty settles, and what it leaves open.

answer.exemplar: A treaty-fixed duty schedule settles the classes of goods, the rate attached to each class, and how collection proceeds. It leaves open how a disputed shipment is classified, how its value is assessed, and how the text is read in a hard case.

questions.explanation: A schedule fixes the classes of goods and the rates attached to them so nobody renegotiates them case by case. What stays open is classification, valuation, and interpretation of the text in disputes.
questions.hint: Separate what the treaty set from what it left.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Jurisdiction moved out of the country
questions.learningObjective: Assess the effect of transferring an office abroad

stimulus.body: The board memo of 11 March records that a coastal mining registry was transferred to a neighbouring administration under a joint-venture instrument. Signatories keep the right to hear disputes arising from the registry. Domestic courts are told to suspend routine hearings until a transfer protocol is signed.

questions.stem: Ticket 216 asks the team to assess what the memo implies about jurisdiction once the registry left the country.

options.text: Jurisdiction moved with the office, so domestic courts must keep hearing every dispute that came to them.
options.misconception: believes jurisdiction never leaves with an office

options.text: Jurisdiction moved abroad with the registry, leaving domestic courts only what the protocol preserves.
Jurisdiction is now shared equally between the two governments because the instrument was a joint venture.
options.misconception: thinks a joint venture splits jurisdiction evenly

options.text: Jurisdiction did not move at all, since the protocol still awaits ratification by the national legislature.
options.misconception: assumes no transfer occurs without ratification

questions.explanation: Moving the registry to another country moves the authority that hears its disputes along with it. Domestic courts keep only what the transfer protocol preserves, so their former reach narrows.
questions.hint: Ask which authority now hears the registry's disputes.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A ministry's account read against a local return
questions.learningObjective: Compare two official records covering the same period

stimulus.body: The ministry ledger for the quarter records grain shipments to four provinces. The local return filed in the same quarter lists six provinces but records only half the tonnage. A note appended to the ledger asks that the difference be explained before the figures are circulated.

questions.stem: Ticket 217 asks the team to read the ministry ledger against the local return and say what it shows.

options.text: The local return is right, since local officials counted the harvest in the fields themselves.
options.misconception: trusts local counts as direct observation

options.text: The ledger is right, since only the ministry is allowed to count shipments for quarterly reporting.
options.misconception: assumes only the ministry may count shipments

options.text: The two records disagree on provinces and tonnage, so the gap must be reconciled before use.
The gap is ordinary seasonal variation in tonnage and needs no explanation beyond a footnote.
options.misconception: reads any variance as routine seasonality

questions.explanation: Both records cover the same quarter but disagree on provinces and tonnage. Neither is self-authenticating, so the gap must be reconciled rather than written off as seasonal.
questions.hint: A disagreement between records is work, not an answer.

questions.topic: A find that set a larger claim in motion
questions.learningObjective: Build an account of how evidence starts a larger argument
questions.stem: Ticket 218 asks the team to build a short account of how one find in a provincial archive can set a larger claim in motion.

options.text: A find counts only if it names a ruler, since claims have always been settled by whoever held the crown.
options.misconception: thinks archival finds matter only for royal titles

options.text: A find counts only if it is older than every earlier document, since antiquity alone settles priority.
options.misconception: believes antiquity by itself establishes priority

options.text: A find counts only if rival states agree to it, so a unilateral discovery carries no legal weight.
options.misconception: assumes a claim needs rivals' consent to count

options.text: A find can reopen a settled claim by supplying evidence, a date, or a legal title others had assumed fixed.

questions.explanation: A find rarely settles a claim; it supplies evidence that changes how an existing claim is understood. Its effect is indirect but real, since later arguments now have material to point to.
questions.hint: Trace the chain from evidence to argument.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rule that stops working where the ground does
questions.learningObjective: Apply a rule whose factual assumption has failed
questions.stem: Ticket 219 asks which reading of a rule handles a case where the physical ground has already moved away from the rule's assumption.

options.text: The rule reads against the situation it was written to govern, since its premise has plainly failed.
The rule applies only where the ground still matches, and the case falls outside it entirely.
options.misconception: treats a failed premise as total exclusion

options.text: The rule applies and the court adds an exception for every place the ground has shifted.
options.misconception: believes courts manufacture exceptions freely

options.text: The rule applies unchanged, because a rule's wording outranks the condition it was written for.
options.misconception: treats wording as immune to its own premise

questions.explanation: A rule built on a factual assumption loses force where that assumption fails. The court reads it against the situation it was meant to govern instead of ignoring or inventing exceptions.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the rule was assumption.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The kind of claim a coastal state makes
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the rights a coastal state may press
questions.stem: Ticket 220 asks for an evaluation of the claim a coastal state can properly make against another state.

answer.exemplar: A coastal state can claim the right to use the belt of water along its shore for passage, to protect its fisheries, and to resist pollution carried to it. It cannot claim the whole sea, exclusive ownership of its resources, or a right to search foreign shipping at will; the claim rests on use, not sovereignty.

questions.explanation: A coastal state's claim rests on its use of the water and on duties owed to it, not on ownership of the sea. So it can claim passage and protection of fisheries, but not dominion over the whole surface.
questions.hint: Ask whether the claim asserts use or ownership.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The line between a protectorate and a colony
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a protectorate from a colony on the evidence

stimulus.body: Article 4 of the regulation states that the territory shall be administered for the convenience of the protecting power, that the local ruler retains the form of government, and that the protecting power may legislate on foreign affairs and trade. A later note observes that the document never mentions ownership.

questions.stem: Ticket 221 asks the team to classify the territory described in the regulation.

options.text: It is a colony, because the protecting power legislates on trade and foreign affairs for it.
options.misconception: treats reserved powers as evidence of ownership

options.text: It is a colony, because the local ruler has been stripped of any real governmental authority.
options.misconception: equates nominal local rule with actual power

options.text: It is a protectorate, because local rulers remain in place while certain outside powers are reserved.
It is an independent state, because the regulation never mentions ownership of the territory.
options.misconception: reads silence about ownership as full sovereignty

questions.explanation: A protectorate keeps local rulers in place while the protecting power reserves certain fields. Here local government survives and only trade and foreign affairs are reserved, which is not ownership.
questions.hint: Look at who governs and who reserves powers.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An exemption offset by charges on others
questions.learningObjective: Separate an exemption from a charge collected alongside it

stimulus.body: A notice to the merchant states that the tea listed in schedule three is exempt from the ordinary duty for the year. Below it, a second line records a harbour charge of two shillings per ton on the same cargo, together with a note that the charge is collected on tonnage landed.

questions.stem: Ticket 222 asks whether the exemption in the notice displaces the harbour charge on the same cargo.

options.text: Yes, because exemption from the duty frees the cargo from every charge collected alongside it.
options.misconception: believes exemption wipes out all related charges

options.text: Yes, because the harbour charge is a duty in substance and the schedule exempts all tea.
options.misconception: equates every levy with a duty for exemption purposes

options.text: No, because the harbour charge is fixed by treaty and no schedule can touch a treaty rate.
options.misconception: assumes treaty rates outrank national schedules

options.text: No, because the exemption removes the duty while the harbour charge is a separate levy on tonnage.

questions.explanation: The exemption and the harbour charge are two different liabilities, and the notice exempts only the duty. A tonnage levy collected on the same landing therefore stands on its own footing.
questions.hint: Ask what the exemption names and what it does not.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A duty schedule fixed by treaty
questions.learningObjective: Show what a tariff schedule can shape without touching borders
questions.stem: Ticket 223 asks the team to show how a treaty duty schedule can shape a port's trade without fixing anyone's borders.

options.text: By setting rates for named classes of goods, the schedule raises or lowers what a route is worth to trade.
By naming which state owns each stretch of coast, the schedule settles the ownership questions outright.
options.misconception: believes a tariff text can allocate territory

options.text: By fixing the price of every commodity, the schedule removes the need to argue about market value.
options.misconception: assumes tariffs fix commodity prices directly

options.text: By granting a monopoly company the right to trade, the schedule guarantees steady customs income.
options.misconception: assumes a tariff schedule always grants a monopoly

questions.explanation: A schedule works on value, not territory: it sets what each class of goods costs to move, and prices shape where trade goes. It settles nothing about ownership and fixes no commodity prices.
questions.hint: Ask whether prices or borders are being set.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Jurisdiction moved out of the country
questions.learningObjective: Determine the reach of home courts after a transfer abroad
questions.stem: Ticket 224 asks what happens to a country's courts when an office that hears disputes is moved to another state.

options.text: The courts keep everything they had, because a transfer of staff cannot alter a court's competence.
options.misconception: thinks moving staff cannot change competence

options.text: The courts keep only what the instrument of transfer preserves, and their reach narrows accordingly.
The courts lose all jurisdiction, because jurisdiction over a matter cannot be split between states.
options.misconception: assumes jurisdiction is all-or-nothing across states

options.text: The courts lose all jurisdiction, because the receiving state now refuses to recognise home judgements.
options.misconception: assumes the receiving state rejects foreign judgements

questions.explanation: Transferring an office transfers the authority it exercises, so the home courts' competence shrinks to whatever the instrument preserves. Neither total retention nor total loss follows from the move alone.
questions.hint: Read the instrument of transfer, not the building.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A ministry's account read against a local return
questions.learningObjective: Design a method for reconciling two official records
questions.stem: Ticket 225 asks for a method that lets the team compare a ministry's account with a local return and reach a defensible figure.

answer.exemplar: Set the two records side by side for the same period, align them by district and by commodity, and list every difference in quantity, date, and classification. Then check the third source that both ought to match, such as the market receipts, and resolve each discrepancy on its own evidence before adopting one figure for the account.

questions.explanation: A defensible comparison lines the accounts up by period and by item, then explains each difference on its own evidence. Adopting one record wholesale, or averaging the two, hides the cause of the gap.
questions.hint: Align period and item, then test each gap.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A find that set a larger claim in motion
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the evidential weight of an archival find

stimulus.body: A clerk's note records that a survey in the northern districts had uncovered a granite marker with a dated inscription naming a grant of land by name. The note adds that the document was copied into a court register some decades after the survey, and that a copy was later produced in a foreign archive.

questions.stem: Ticket 226 asks the team to weigh what the note implies about the larger claim the marker set in motion.

options.text: It settles the claim, because an inscribed granite marker cannot be forged and proves the grant.
options.misconception: believes a physical marker proves the grant outright

options.text: It settles nothing, because the inscription's dating depends entirely on the clerk's handwriting.
options.misconception: dismisses a find on handwriting alone

options.text: It supports the claim only if the marker was dug up inside the disputed territory by its own government.
options.misconception: requires the find to be made by the claimant

options.text: It gave the claim new material to argue from, though its date and transmission still need testing.

questions.explanation: A dated marker naming a grant gives a claim something to point to, so a larger argument begins to move. It is not self-proving: the dating, the copying and the copy found abroad need checking.
questions.hint: Ask whether the find settles or only supplies.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rule that stops working where the ground does
questions.learningObjective: Read an unamended rule against changed ground

stimulus.body: A notice says that the embankment must hold the tide back to the level marked on the 1840 survey. A survey made last spring shows the shoreline now sits a hundred paces seaward of that mark, and the ditch that once carried the overflow has silted up. The notice has not been amended since it was issued.

questions.stem: Ticket 227 asks how the notice should now be read, given what the newer survey shows.

options.text: Against the situation it was written for, since the physical premise on which it rests has failed.
Literally and without change, since an unamended notice binds regardless of what the ground does.
options.misconception: believes wording outranks physical reality

options.text: Only where the shoreline still matches the 1840 mark, and nowhere else at all.
options.misconception: treats a failed premise as complete exclusion

options.text: As though the writer had intended the newer shoreline, since a court reads for its purpose.
options.misconception: assumes courts always read for a purpose

questions.explanation: The notice was framed on a physical condition that no longer holds, so it must be read against the situation it was written for. A literal reading would apply a level the ground can no longer meet.
questions.hint: Ask which stated condition has ceased to be true.

questions.stem: Ticket 228 asks the team to set out the claim a coastal state may make where a foreign fleet fishes inside its waters.

options.text: A claim to seize the fishing vessels outright, since the fish have always belonged to the shore.
options.misconception: believes fishing gives a right of seizure

options.text: A claim to protect its fisheries and preserve its own rights in the sea, not to own the water.
A claim to close the whole sea to foreign fleets, since the closing line may be drawn anywhere.
options.misconception: thinks a state may close the whole sea

options.text: A claim to seize the fleet's catch and share the proceeds with the coastal treasury.
options.misconception: assumes a state may take a rival's catch

questions.explanation: A coastal state claims rights over its own use and against pollution, not ownership of the sea. Seizure of foreign vessels and catch would exceed those rights, which rest on use and on duties owed.
questions.hint: Ask whether the claim is use-based or ownership-based.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The line between a protectorate and a colony
questions.learningObjective: State the legal test separating a protectorate from a colony
questions.stem: Ticket 229 asks for the distinction that separates a protectorate from a colony in a legal instrument.

options.text: A protectorate keeps a foreign army in the territory, while a colony does not allow any foreign troops.
options.misconception: makes troop presence the deciding test

options.text: A protectorate grants trade privileges to the protecting power, while a colony grants none at all.
options.misconception: makes trade privileges the deciding test

options.text: A protectorate keeps local rulers in place, while a colony transfers the government itself.
A protectorate is administered from abroad, while a colony must be administered by local officials.
options.misconception: reads the label as the whole test

questions.explanation: The turning point is who governs: a protectorate keeps the local ruler and reserves some fields, while a colony transfers government. Trade terms and troops may vary without changing that.
questions.hint: Ask who holds the government in each case.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An exemption offset by charges on others
questions.learningObjective: Read an assessment roll to separate relief from other charges

A second column, headed with the word charges, lists levies still collected on the same producers, each entered against a separate heading.

options.text: The exemption has removed every charge from the district, so the second column must be a copy error.
options.misconception: reads a surviving charge as a clerical error

options.text: The exemption never took effect, because the roll lists the article rather than granting relief.
options.misconception: thinks exemption needs a separate granting instrument

options.text: The exemption applies to the article only, while the other charges fall on the producers generally.
options.misconception: believes exemption always reaches every levy

options.text: The exemption covers the named article, while the other charges stand against the producers as such.

questions.explanation: The roll grants relief on one article and then lists charges under other headings, showing they are separate liabilities. Relief from the duty does not travel to levies on the producers generally.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A duty schedule fixed by treaty
questions.learningObjective: Say what a schedule settles and what it reserves

stimulus.body: The schedule opens with a list of goods, each given a numbered class and a rate expressed as a fraction of the value. A note at the end states that the classes are exhaustive for the purposes of the schedule and that goods not listed are to be valued by the old local practice. A covering instruction asks that the schedule be read as a complete code for the listed goods.

questions.stem: Ticket 231 asks the team to say what the schedule does and does not settle about duty.

options.text: It fixes the classes and their rates, while leaving unlisted goods to the older local practice.
It fixes the classes and their rates, and also determines the value of every unlisted good.
options.misconception: thinks the schedule also fixes valuations

options.text: It fixes only the rates, leaving the team free to decide which goods fall into each class.
options.misconception: believes the classes themselves are negotiable

options.text: It fixes nothing at all, because a schedule cannot bind customs officers in practice.
options.misconception: assumes a written schedule has no effect

questions.explanation: The schedule is a code for the goods it lists: class and rate are settled there. Unlisted goods are expressly left to the older practice, so neither their classification nor valuation is settled.
questions.hint: Read the closing note on unlisted goods.

options.text: Existing disputes continue untouched, since a change of forum never disturbs a case already begun.
options.misconception: assumes pending cases are never affected

options.text: Disputes already before the forum are affected, because the forum's authority over them has moved too.
Existing disputes fall at once, because the new state need not recognise anything said in court.
options.misconception: thinks a transfer voids pending proceedings outright

options.text: Existing disputes must be restarted before the home courts, since their old rulings become void.
options.misconception: assumes old rulings are void after a transfer

questions.explanation: A transfer moves the authority handling pending disputes, so their footing changes with it. The cases are neither frozen in place nor voided outright; the instrument must settle their footing.

questions.stem: Ticket 233 asks what a ministry's account proves when it is read against a local return covering the same period.

options.text: It proves the ministry is right, since a central account is compiled with better records than any local one.
options.misconception: assumes a central account is always better

options.text: It proves the local return is wrong, since the ministry alone holds the full picture of the quarter.
options.misconception: assumes the ministry alone sees the full picture

options.text: It proves only where the two records agree; where they differ, the difference needs its own inquiry.
It proves nothing either way, since no account can be checked against any other record.
options.misconception: believes no record can ever be cross-checked

questions.explanation: Agreement between the two records is established where they match. Where they differ, the divergence is itself the finding, and must be investigated rather than settled by rank.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A find that set a larger claim in motion
questions.learningObjective: Describe the sequence by which a find becomes a state claim
questions.stem: Ticket 234 asks the team to describe, in order, how a find in an archive can grow into a claim asserted by two governments.

answer.exemplar: The sequence usually runs: a find surfaces in a local archive; specialists date it and argue over its authenticity; a government claims it shows a title or a grant; a second government either accepts the claim, counters it with older evidence, or offers a different reading; and the dispute is then handed to mediation, arbitration, or settled by force. Each step adds a fact that the next step depends on.

questions.explanation: The find feeds a chain: dating, authenticity, a government's claim, a rival's response, then settlement. Missing that sequence hides the point that the find alone never carries a claim.
questions.hint: List the steps that carry the claim forward.

options.misconception: treats a changed condition as complete exclusion

options.text: The statute applies to the new channel automatically, since the statute governs waters and not courses.
options.misconception: assumes the statute follows the water itself

questions.explanation: The schedule describes the river as surveyed, and a later diversion has broken that description. The statute must then be read against the new ground rather than applied to a course that no longer exists.
questions.hint: Compare the schedule's wording with today's ground.

questions.explanation: An exemption offsets the liability it names, not the whole account, and a charge on a different shipment stands on its own footing. Recording each on its own line keeps the effect of each visible.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A duty schedule fixed by treaty
questions.learningObjective: Explain who may amend a treaty duty schedule
questions.stem: Ticket 239 asks for an explanation of why a treaty duty schedule could be changed only by the states that made the treaty.

answer.exemplar: The schedule binds the states that agreed it, so its terms can be altered only with their consent. A later arrangement among outsiders cannot rewrite those rates for the parties, though it may add new terms for those who join it. For a state that never acceded, the schedule simply does not bind it at all.

questions.explanation: A treaty binds its parties, so only they can change the terms they agreed. Outsiders may make their own arrangements among themselves, and states that never acceded are not bound by it.
questions.hint: Ask who is bound before asking who may change it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Jurisdiction moved out of the country
questions.learningObjective: Locate jurisdiction from a transfer article and its protocol

stimulus.body: Article 7 provides that the registry and its archives shall be transferred to the administration named in the schedule, and that disputes arising from entries made before the transfer shall be heard by the tribunal designated in the same article. A protocol signed two years later lists the categories of entry the designated tribunal will accept, and closes the list with the words and such other matters as the parties agree in writing.

questions.stem: Ticket 240 asks the team to read the article and protocol and say where jurisdiction now lies.

options.text: With the domestic courts, since the protocol adds categories without removing the tribunal's role.
options.misconception: assumes later protocol restores home jurisdiction

options.text: With the designated tribunal for the listed categories, and with the parties by agreement beyond them.
With the receiving administration's ordinary courts, since the tribunal was set up only for entry disputes.
options.misconception: assumes the tribunal handles every kind of case

options.text: Nowhere in particular, since a protocol that closes a list cannot establish a forum at all.
options.misconception: believes a closed list defeats any forum

questions.explanation: The article moves the registry and names the tribunal for pre-transfer disputes, and the protocol sets its reach by list. Beyond the list, jurisdiction depends on what the parties agree in writing.
questions.hint: Read the closing words of the protocol list.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A ministry's account read against a local return
questions.learningObjective: Explain a gap between two totals once a counting basis is known

stimulus.body: The ministry return gives total tonnage for the season as eighteen thousand quarters. The local return gives eleven thousand, and its supporting sheets itemise deliveries by farm and by day. A clerk's memorandum notes that the local figure counts only carted grain and that grain carried by water was tallied separately in a sheet not attached to the return.

questions.stem: Ticket 241 asks the team to say what the two returns show once the clerk's note is read.

options.text: The ministry figure is correct, since the local return plainly omits most of what was harvested.
options.misconception: jumps to the ministry figure as correct

options.text: The local figure is correct, since a return should count only what passed along the cart roads.
options.misconception: accepts a narrower count as the whole count

options.text: The two totals measure different things, so they can only be compared once the basis of each is fixed.
Neither figure can be used, since a memorandum about counting methods has invalidated both returns.
options.misconception: concludes a method note voids both returns

questions.explanation: The gap is explained by what each return counts, not by error on either side. Until the basis of each figure is fixed and stated, the two totals are not comparable numbers.
questions.hint: Ask what each figure counts before comparing them.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A find that set a larger claim in motion
questions.learningObjective: Judge when an archival find strengthens a claim
questions.stem: Ticket 242 asks the team to judge when an archival find strengthens a claim and when it merely creates noise.

options.text: When it is dramatic, since finds that make headlines carry more weight than quiet ones.
options.misconception: judges a find by how dramatic it is

options.text: When it is new to the world, since a find already known to scholars changes nothing at all.
options.misconception: believes a known find changes nothing

options.text: When it supports the claim that is already accepted, since new evidence for the winner helps.
options.misconception: values evidence only when it backs the accepted view

options.text: When it bears on the element the claim rests on, and its dating and transmission can be checked.

questions.explanation: A find strengthens a claim when it bears on the element it depends on and can be tested for date and transmission. Drama and novelty add weight the evidence itself does not carry.
questions.hint: Ask which element the claim actually needs.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rule that stops working where the ground does
questions.learningObjective: Identify the consequence of a failed factual assumption
questions.stem: Ticket 243 asks which consequence follows when the factual assumption under a rule has failed in the territory where it is applied.

options.text: The rule is read against the situation it was framed for, so that its purpose survives the change.
The rule lapses entirely, since a rule cannot survive the failure of its own premise.
options.misconception: believes a failed premise voids the rule entirely

options.text: The rule applies as written, since only the legislature can respond to a change of circumstance.
options.misconception: assumes courts cannot adjust to changed facts

options.text: A new rule is created for the territory, since old rules never reach new ground.
options.misconception: assumes courts create replacement rules

questions.explanation: Read against its original purpose, a rule can still do useful work where the premise has changed. Lapsing it, applying it literally, or inventing a replacement are separate errors.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule was for, not just what it says.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The kind of claim a coastal state makes
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a coastal state does not claim ownership of the sea
questions.stem: Ticket 244 asks for an explanation of why the claim of a coastal state is not a claim to own the sea.

answer.exemplar: The sea is too large and too shared for any coastal state to hold it as territory, and the practice of states long recognised that a narrow belt along the shore may be used for passage and that fisheries and the shore may be protected. Ownership of the whole surface would also require excluding every other user, which no state has the means or the right to do.

questions.explanation: The claim is limited to a belt of use and protection of fisheries and shore, which is what states assert in practice. Ownership of the whole surface would require excluding every other user.
questions.hint: Ask whether the claim is about use or about the surface.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The line between a protectorate and a colony
questions.learningObjective: Classify a territory from a governor's report

stimulus.body: The report states that the protecting power appointed a governor for the territory and that the governor alone issued the ordinances and the permits. It adds that the local council met only to advise, and that its decisions were recorded but not given effect without the governor's approval. The report closes by listing revenue collected in the territory and sent to the protecting power's treasury.

questions.stem: Ticket 245 asks the team to say what this arrangement is and to give the reason.

options.text: It is a protectorate, since the local council was retained in the form it already had.
options.misconception: reads a retained council as a protectorate

options.text: It is a trade post, since the arrangement concerns revenue rather than government.
options.misconception: confuses a trading station with a colony

options.text: It is a colony, because the protecting power governs directly and the local council only advises.
It is a mandate, because the local council advised while the governor was appointed.
options.misconception: assumes a local council implies a mandate

questions.explanation: The test is who governs, and here the appointed governor alone issued binding orders while the local council only advised. Direct government with an advisory council is the colonial arrangement.
questions.hint: Ask who issued the binding orders here.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An exemption offset by charges on others
questions.learningObjective: Answer a marginal question on exemption and storage charges

stimulus.body: The docket shows a claim of exemption for one cask of salt entered under the general heading of goods in bond. A second entry records a storage charge on the same cask, and a marginal note asks the collector to state whether the exemption extends to the charge because both entries concern the same barrel.

questions.stem: Ticket 246 asks the team to answer the collector's marginal question.

options.text: Yes, because the charge and the exemption both concern the same barrel and so share one fate.
options.misconception: extends exemption to charges on the same goods

options.text: Yes, because all charges on goods in bond are waived whenever a bond is broken under exemption.
options.misconception: believes breaking a bond waives all charges

options.text: No, because a storage charge is a service the merchant has actually used and paid for.
options.misconception: treats a storage charge as a customs duty

options.text: No, because the exemption covers the duty on the salt and not a charge for storing the cask.

questions.explanation: The exemption names a duty on the salt; a storage charge for holding the cask is a separate liability for a service rendered. Sharing one barrel does not merge the two liabilities.
questions.hint: Ask whether the exemption names this charge at all.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A duty schedule fixed by treaty
questions.learningObjective: Weigh what a duty schedule achieves and cannot achieve
questions.stem: Ticket 247 asks the team to weigh what a treaty duty schedule can and cannot achieve for the states that signed it.

options.text: It can stabilise what trade costs, which lets firms plan, but it cannot settle what the trade is worth.
It can settle what the trade is worth, since fixed rates tell producers exactly who should buy.
options.misconception: believes fixed rates fix market demand

options.text: It cannot stabilise anything, since rates in a schedule are routinely ignored at the custom house.
options.misconception: assumes written rates are routinely ignored

options.text: It settles both cost and value, because a schedule is binding on everyone who trades in the ports.
options.misconception: believes a schedule binds non-parties too

questions.explanation: A schedule fixes charges, which eases the uncertainty that hampers planning, but says nothing about demand or who should buy. It binds those who agreed it and does not settle what any trade is worth.
questions.hint: Ask what a rate can and cannot tell you.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Jurisdiction moved out of the country
questions.learningObjective: State the effect of a transfer on the reach of home courts
questions.stem: Ticket 248 asks which statement about jurisdiction after an office has been moved abroad is correct.

options.text: The home courts keep their reach, since a transfer changes the staff but not the authority.
options.misconception: believes a transfer leaves authority behind

options.text: The home courts reach only what the instrument of transfer preserves for them, and no more.
The home courts lose everything, since the office's authority cannot be split across a border.
options.misconception: assumes authority cannot be divided

options.text: The receiving state's courts take everything, since they now host the office and its archive.
options.misconception: assumes hosting an office transfers all cases

questions.explanation: Jurisdiction follows the authority, and authority transferred with the office, so the home forum keeps only what the instrument preserves. Neither total loss nor total capture follows from the move.
questions.hint: Read the instrument's savings clause.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A ministry's account read against a local return
questions.learningObjective: State the purpose of a ministry account and a local return
questions.stem: Ticket 249 asks for a short statement of what a ministry account and a local return are each meant to record.

answer.exemplar: A ministry account is the central record, compiled from returns gathered from districts, and it exists to give the government a single figure for the whole country. A local return is the district's own record of what was produced, collected, or shipped within its own borders, made by local officers and often kept for local purposes before any central use.

questions.explanation: The two records are made for different purposes and at different levels, which is why they can differ without either being wrong. One aggregates; the other reports one place in its own terms.
questions.hint: Ask what each record was made to do.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A find that set a larger claim in motion
questions.learningObjective: Assess what correspondence shows about a find's standing

stimulus.body: A letter from the provincial office states that a tombstone recovered during road work carries a line naming a village and a grant of land made by a governor whose seal the office recognises. A second letter, written two years later, asks the ministry to confirm whether the same tombstone appears in a printed list of antiquities compiled abroad.

questions.stem: Ticket 250 asks the team to say what the correspondence shows about the find's standing.

options.text: The find is conclusive, because a recognised seal proves the grant was made as described.
options.misconception: treats a seal as conclusive proof

options.text: The find is worthless, because road work cannot be trusted to record what it uncovers.
options.misconception: dismisses finds by where they were uncovered

options.text: The find is already published, since the second letter refers to a printed list.
options.misconception: confuses a query with a printed record

options.text: The find is real and locally credible, but its wider history is still being checked.

questions.explanation: The tombstone is credible evidence given the recognised seal, and the letter seeking confirmation shows the record being checked against outside lists. That does not settle the find's wider history.
questions.hint: A question in a letter is not an answer.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rule that stops working where the ground does
questions.learningObjective: Apply a canal requirement after the bed has silted up

stimulus.body: The statute directs that the canal shall be kept deep enough to carry water to the mills on the upper branch. An engineer's report notes that silt has raised the bed of the upper branch by two feet since the statute was written, and that the mills now receive less water than the statute assumes.

questions.stem: Ticket 251 asks how the statute's requirement should now be applied to the upper branch.

options.text: As a requirement to preserve the purpose of carrying water to the mills, adjusted to the silted bed.
As a fixed depth of two feet more than before, since the statute's figure is unchanged.
options.misconception: applies the original figure without adjustment

options.text: As satisfied, since the statute says nothing about how much water the mills receive.
options.misconception: reads the statute as satisfied by form

options.text: As void, since a statute cannot govern a canal whose physical conditions have changed.
options.misconception: treats changed conditions as voiding a statute

questions.explanation: The statute was framed on a bed depth that has changed, so it is read against present ground to keep doing its work. Keeping the old figure or calling the statute satisfied misses that.
questions.hint: Ask what the requirement was for.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The kind of claim a coastal state makes
questions.learningObjective: Explain why coastal powers disagreed about the width of the belt
questions.stem: Ticket 252 asks the team to set out why coastal powers disagreed about how wide the usable belt of sea should be.

options.text: Because each read the law of the sea as fixed by treaty, and treaty terms were interpreted differently.
options.misconception: blames treaty interpretation for every disagreement

options.text: Because the belt is a practical limit, and states with different coasts and fleets drew it differently.
Because the older rules favoured whichever state had the longer coastline, and every state knew it.
options.misconception: claims older rules simply favoured longer coasts

options.text: Because the question had no settled law behind it, so every state claimed whatever suited it.
options.misconception: assumes the law was simply unsettled

questions.explanation: The belt is a practical working limit, not a fixed line, so states with different coasts and fleets drew it differently. Calling it settled law or mere bad faith misses that practical character.
questions.hint: Ask how each coast differs in use.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The line between a protectorate and a colony
questions.learningObjective: State what follows when the government is moved out and staffed directly
questions.stem: Ticket 253 asks what follows for a territory once a protecting power moves its government out and staffs the territory directly.

options.text: It remains a protectorate, because the local council still meets and still records its views.
options.misconception: treats an advisory council as decisive

options.text: It becomes a colony, since the government has been transferred out and is run by foreign officers.
It becomes an independent state, since direct administration removes any foreign involvement.
options.misconception: thinks direct administration grants independence

options.text: It becomes a trading post, since the revenue now goes to the protecting power's treasury.
options.misconception: confuses treasury arrangements with status

questions.explanation: Transferring the government out and staffing it directly moves a territory from protectorate to colony, whatever the local council still does. Neither a council nor a treasury arrangement settles status.
questions.hint: Ask who staffs the government now.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An exemption offset by charges on others
questions.learningObjective: Explain why relief for one class leaves other liabilities untouched
questions.stem: Ticket 254 asks for an explanation of why an exemption granted to one class of merchants does not shift the whole burden of charges onto others.

answer.exemplar: An exemption relieves the holders of the named class from the duty on the goods they bring, and it does so without changing what anyone else owes. The charges falling on other merchants keep the same rates, the same assessment, and the same collection. A general surcharge, by contrast, is spread deliberately across the whole trade and would not be an exemption at all.

questions.explanation: Relief granted to one class leaves other merchants' liabilities as they were, because exemption changes one entry, not the structure. A general surcharge, spread deliberately, is a different instrument.
questions.hint: Ask what changed and for whom.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A duty schedule fixed by treaty
questions.learningObjective: Weigh what a schedule header and accession clause establish

stimulus.body: The schedule is headed with the names of the five states that made it and the year of signature, followed by a list of classes with their rates. An article in the same treaty provides that the schedule may be amended by the consent of the states that made it, and that a state acceding later accepts the schedule as it stands at the moment of accession.

questions.stem: Ticket 255 asks the team to weigh what the header and article together establish.

options.text: The schedule binds its makers, and a later accession takes the rates as they stand at that moment.
The schedule binds any state that trades with the parties, whether it acceded or not.
options.misconception: believes a schedule binds all trading states

options.text: The schedule can be amended by any single party, since each state keeps its own customs.
options.misconception: assumes one party may amend a treaty schedule

options.text: The schedule expires when a new state accedes, since accession revives the earlier rates.
options.misconception: thinks accession revives old rates

questions.explanation: The header names the parties and the article fixes amendment and accession, so the schedule binds its makers and freezes for an acceder at the rates then standing.
questions.hint: Read the accession clause carefully.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Jurisdiction moved out of the country
questions.learningObjective: Read an administrative circular about a moved office

stimulus.body: The circular announces that the office of the registrar has been moved to the neighbouring country and that its staff have gone with it. It instructs officers at home to continue collecting fees on the old schedule until the transfer protocol is issued, and it closes with a note that no change of authority is intended by the collection instruction.

questions.stem: Ticket 256 asks the team to say what the circular establishes about jurisdiction.

options.text: Home courts keep full jurisdiction, because the circular instructs officers to keep working as before.
options.misconception: reads administrative continuity as legal continuity

options.text: Jurisdiction has moved with the office, and the collection instruction changes nothing about that.
Jurisdiction is split between both countries, since officers on each side keep some duties.
options.misconception: assumes shared duties create shared jurisdiction

options.text: Jurisdiction stayed put, because the transfer protocol has not yet been signed by anyone.
options.misconception: treats unsigned protocols as preserving jurisdiction

questions.explanation: The office and its staff have moved, so the authority to hear disputes has moved too. An instruction to keep collecting fees is administrative continuity, and the circular says it changes no authority.
questions.hint: Ask what actually moved.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A ministry's account read against a local return
questions.learningObjective: Weigh how far a disagreement between two records can be used
questions.stem: Ticket 257 asks the team to weigh how far a disagreement between a ministry account and a local return can be used.

options.text: It should be ignored, since two sets of figures for one quarter always disagree by habit.
options.misconception: assumes two records always disagree

options.text: It should be averaged, since the truth always lies halfway between two official counts.
options.misconception: believes the truth is the midpoint of two counts

options.text: It should be resolved item by item, so each difference is explained on its own evidence.
It should be escalated, since only a minister can decide which of two accounts is right.
options.misconception: believes only a minister may resolve a discrepancy

questions.explanation: A gap between two records becomes useful when each difference is traced and explained on its own evidence. Ignoring it, averaging it, or escalating it instead of inquiring avoids the work.
questions.hint: Ask how each difference would be explained.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A find that set a larger claim in motion
questions.learningObjective: Identify the finding that most changes a claim's position
questions.stem: Ticket 258 asks which finding in an archive most changes the position of a state pursuing a larger claim.

options.text: A document confirming that an earlier treaty was signed on the date usually given.
options.misconception: values confirmation of known dates above all else

options.text: A report describing the wealth of the territory at the time the claim began.
options.misconception: treats economic description as decisive

options.text: A letter from a foreign scholar praising the quality of the archive's holdings.
options.misconception: treats foreign praise as evidence

options.text: A record that grants the very title the claim asserts to a party the claim excludes.

questions.explanation: A record granting the claimed title to an excluded party attacks the claim at its core and forces its terms or dating to be reconsidered. Descriptions and praise leave the disputed element alone.
questions.hint: Ask whether it touches the element in dispute.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rule that stops working where the ground does
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a court handles a rule with a failed premise
questions.stem: Ticket 259 asks for an account of how a court decides what to do with a rule whose factual premise has failed.

answer.exemplar: The court first identifies the assumption of fact on which the rule was framed, then checks the evidence to see whether that assumption still holds where the rule is being applied. If it does not, the court reads the rule against the purpose it was meant to serve and applies it so as to keep that purpose alive, noting in the judgment which fact has changed and why the literal wording no longer fits.

questions.explanation: The sequence is: find the premise, test it against the facts, then read the rule against its purpose and explain the change. Literal application or declaring the rule spent skips the test.
questions.hint: Find the premise, then test it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The kind of claim a coastal state makes
questions.learningObjective: Weigh what a minute shows about the nature of the coastal claim

stimulus.body: A minute from the foreign office notes that two delegations have proposed different outer limits for the belt of sea each claims along its own shore, one measured from the harbour mouth and the other from the outermost fishing village. The minute asks whether a compromise line might be adopted that both could accept.

questions.stem: Ticket 260 asks the team to weigh what the minute shows about the nature of the coastal claim.

options.text: The claim is a fixed line already agreed, so the difference is only a drafting error.
options.misconception: assumes the limit was already agreed

options.text: The claim is a practical limit drawn differently by each state, so compromise is the realistic route.
The claim is a matter of strict title, so the wider line belongs to whoever can prove it.
options.misconception: reads the belt as a question of strict title

options.text: The claim has no legal content, since two proposals prove that no rule governs the matter.
options.misconception: concludes disagreement means no rule exists

questions.explanation: Each state proposes the limit its own coast and fleet make workable, the mark of a practical claim rather than a fixed line or strict title. That is why compromise is a realistic route.
questions.hint: Ask why each number differs.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The line between a protectorate and a colony
questions.learningObjective: Read a sequence of files showing a change of status

stimulus.body: The file contains a treaty granting the coastal ruler the right to govern his own affairs, and it names the foreign power as protector. A later file records a commission that surveyed the country's interior and set out districts for administration, and a third paper records the appointment of provincial commissioners with power to issue ordinances.

questions.stem: Ticket 261 asks the team to say what the sequence in the file shows.

options.text: A protectorate held throughout, since the first treaty is never meant to be superseded.
options.misconception: assumes the first instrument governs forever

options.text: A colony from the start, since later files merely give detail to what the treaty began.
options.misconception: reads later detail as original intent

options.text: A protectorate that became a colony once districts were set and commissioners appointed.
Two unrelated governments, since nothing in the files links one arrangement to the other.
options.misconception: sees no continuity between the arrangements

questions.explanation: The treaty establishing a protectorate came first, and later papers show districts with commissioners empowered to rule. That is how a protectorate gives way to a colony.
questions.hint: Read the files in date order.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An exemption offset by charges on others
questions.learningObjective: Build guidance on presenting an exemption and surrounding charges
questions.stem: Ticket 262 asks the team to build a short guidance note on how to present an exemption and the charges around it.

options.text: Show the exemption first, then list every charge, so the relief appears as the largest figure.
options.misconception: orders entries to flatter the relief

options.text: Show the charges only, since the exemption is an administrative detail for the file, not the account.
options.misconception: hides relief from the account

options.text: Show the net figure only, since the parties are interested in the amount payable and nothing else.
options.misconception: reduces the note to a net number

options.text: Show each entry against the shipment it belongs to, with the exemption shown on the shipment it covers.

questions.explanation: Showing each entry against its own shipment keeps relief visible and charges separately assessable. Ordering by size, hiding relief, or collapsing to a net figure destroys that.
questions.hint: Keep every entry checkable on its own.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A duty schedule fixed by treaty
questions.learningObjective: Recall the principal contents of a treaty duty schedule
questions.stem: Ticket 263 asks the team to recall what a treaty duty schedule principally consists of.

options.text: Named classes of goods, each with a rate, arranged for the use of customs officers.
A list of ports where goods may be landed, each with the duties to be paid there.
options.misconception: recalls port lists instead of tariff classes

options.text: A statement of the rates at which goods may be exchanged between the trading states.
options.misconception: confuses customs rates with exchange rates

options.text: An agreement on which court shall hear disputes arising from the goods so classified.
options.misconception: confuses a tariff with a choice of forum

questions.explanation: A duty schedule is a classified list of goods with rates attached, made for customs use. Ports, exchange rates and forum clauses belong to other instruments and are not what the schedule is.
questions.hint: Ask what customs needs to read.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Jurisdiction moved out of the country
questions.learningObjective: Explain what it means for jurisdiction to leave a country
questions.stem: Ticket 264 asks for a plain explanation of what it means for jurisdiction to move out of a country.

answer.exemplar: Jurisdiction is the authority to hear and decide certain matters. When an office or a registry is moved abroad, the authority that office exercised travels with it, and the courts at home are left with only whatever the instrument of transfer keeps for them. That can include earlier decisions, which usually stay valid because they were rightly decided in the proper forum.

questions.explanation: Moving jurisdiction means moving the power to decide, not just the offices where decisions are typed. Only what the instrument preserves stays behind, and earlier decisions typically survive.
questions.hint: Ask what authority is being carried across.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A ministry's account read against a local return
questions.learningObjective: Assess a consolidated figure whose working papers are missing

stimulus.body: The auditor notes that the ministry account shows the quarter's shipments as a single consolidated line, while the district returns that support it are held separately and were not seen by the auditor. An exception note asks whether the consolidated figure can be supported when its working papers are unavailable.

questions.stem: Ticket 265 asks the team to say what the note shows about the ministry account.

options.text: The account is supported, since a consolidated line is the normal form in which quarterly figures appear.
options.misconception: treats form as evidence of correctness

options.text: The account is void, since figures compiled without papers may never be published at all.
options.misconception: jumps to declaring the account void

options.text: The account is unsupported on its face, because the papers that would test it cannot be produced.
The account is provisional, which means it must be published at once and corrected later if needed.
options.misconception: confuses provisional status with a licence to publish

questions.explanation: A consolidated figure that cannot be traced to working papers has nothing to test it against, so it stands unsupported. Declaring it void, or publishing it as provisional, does not answer that.
questions.hint: Ask what would test the figure.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A find that set a larger claim in motion
questions.learningObjective: Weigh a find disturbed by excavation at the site

stimulus.body: The survey report records that a bronze plaque was lifted from a cairn during drainage work, and that the same cairn appears in a drawing made by an earlier survey party twenty years before. The report adds that the drain, once dug, was deliberately backfilled so that the site could not be examined again without further excavation.

questions.stem: Ticket 266 asks the team to weigh what the report shows about the find's evidential value.

options.text: The find is worthless, since the plaque was lifted from a site that was disturbed by drainage.
options.misconception: dismisses a find because of excavation damage

options.text: The find is conclusive, since a bronze plaque in a cairn is proof of a legal grant.
options.misconception: treats the artefact type as proof

options.text: The find is public domain, since an earlier survey party had already drawn the same cairn.
options.misconception: reads an earlier drawing as proof of prior recovery

options.text: The find is weakened, since the site's records were disturbed and no further checking is easy.

questions.explanation: Backfilling and disturbance weaken the find, because the context that would date it is gone. Earlier drawings show the cairn was known, not that the plaque was a grant.
questions.hint: Ask what context the site can still show.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rule that stops working where the ground does
questions.learningObjective: Compare two ways of handling a rule whose ground has shifted
questions.stem: Ticket 267 asks the team to compare two ways of handling a rule whose ground has shifted.

options.text: Reading the rule against its purpose keeps it usable, while literal reading leaves it pointing at nothing.
Literal reading keeps the rule intact, while reading against purpose quietly rewrites what it says.
options.misconception: treats purposive reading as quiet rewriting

options.text: Both readings are equally sound, so the choice can be left to whichever clerk is available.
options.misconception: treats the choice as arbitrary

options.text: Both readings fail, so the rule should be replaced by a fresh one covering the changed ground.
options.misconception: jumps straight to replacing the rule

questions.explanation: Literal reading ties the rule to a failed condition and leaves it inoperative; reading against purpose keeps it doing its framed work. Arbitrary choice or outright replacement avoids the question.
questions.hint: Ask what each reading does with the rule.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The kind of claim a coastal state makes
questions.learningObjective: Identify the claim a coastal state may press over fishing
questions.stem: Ticket 268 asks which claim a coastal state is entitled to press against a foreign fleet fishing in its waters.

options.text: A claim to treat the fleet's presence as a casus belli, since fishing limits are a matter of war.
options.misconception: escalates a fishing dispute into a war claim

options.text: A claim to protect its fisheries and require the dues owed for what the fleet took.
A claim to board every foreign vessel in its waters in search of licences.
options.misconception: asserts a general right of boarding

options.text: A claim to fine the fleet's owners in its own courts without any hearing of the case.
options.misconception: assumes jurisdiction to fine without a hearing

questions.explanation: A coastal state may press its rights over fisheries and dues. Boarding at large and fining unheard claims exceed them, and a fishing dispute is not by itself a casus belli.
questions.hint: Ask what right the state actually holds.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The line between a protectorate and a colony
questions.learningObjective: Analyse why the test of status rests on government
questions.stem: Ticket 269 asks for an analysis of why the distinction between a protectorate and a colony rests on government rather than on trade or finance.

answer.exemplar: Trade concessions and treasury arrangements can be varied or reversed without changing the legal character of a territory, so they cannot be the test. What determines the character is who holds the government: if the local ruler continues to govern while certain fields are reserved, the arrangement is a protectorate; if the government itself is transferred out and staffed by foreign officers, it is a colony.

questions.explanation: The character of a territory turns on who governs it, since trade terms and revenue arrangements vary widely within each category. A retained ruler signals a protectorate; a foreign government a colony.
questions.hint: Ask who holds the government.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An exemption offset by charges on others
questions.learningObjective: Read a warehouse ledger showing exemption and rent separately

stimulus.body: The ledger opens with an entry recording an exemption from the ordinary duty for goods kept in the bonded store, and the column beside it carries a separate figure for the rent of the store. A foot note states that rent is collected on the space occupied and not on the value of the goods.

questions.stem: Ticket 270 asks the team to say how the two figures in the ledger should be read.

options.text: The exemption and the rent are one charge, since both are entered in the same ledger.
options.misconception: merges two charges because they share a book

options.text: They are separate charges, with the exemption covering only the duty on the goods.
The ledger is incomplete, since a store cannot charge rent at all in a bonded district.
options.misconception: believes bonded stores may not charge rent

options.text: The rent is exempt too, since goods under exemption should cost the merchant nothing at all.
options.misconception: extends exemption to every cost of storage

questions.explanation: The note makes clear that rent is charged for space and the exemption for the duty on the goods, so the entries stand independently. Sharing a ledger joins them nowhere.
questions.hint: Read the foot note on what rent covers.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A duty schedule fixed by treaty
questions.learningObjective: Work out which shipments a schedule covers

stimulus.body: A consular report states that the schedule of duties applies to goods shipped from the ports of the states that made the treaty, and that other shipments are assessed under the local practice of the port. It adds that the rates themselves have never been changed since the year of signature.

questions.stem: Ticket 271 asks the team to work out which shipments the schedule covers.

options.text: Only goods shipped from the ports of the states that made the treaty.
All goods landed at any port of a party, whatever their place of shipment.
options.misconception: reads coverage by landing rather than shipment

options.text: All goods entering the ports of a party, including those shipped from elsewhere.
options.misconception: assumes coverage follows the importing state

options.text: Only goods carried by vessels flying the flag of a party state.
options.misconception: reads coverage as following the vessel's flag

questions.explanation: The report ties the schedule to the place of shipment, so it reaches goods shipped from the parties' ports only. Neither the port of landing nor the flag brings other goods within it.
questions.hint: Ask where the goods were shipped from.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Jurisdiction moved out of the country
questions.learningObjective: Set out how to locate jurisdiction after a transfer abroad
questions.stem: Ticket 272 asks the team to set out how to decide where jurisdiction lies after an office has been moved abroad.

options.text: By the receiving state's ordinary practice, since that is where the archive now physically lies.
options.misconception: locates jurisdiction by where the archive sits

options.text: By the instrument of transfer, the forum it names, and any later protocol those two produce.
By asking which forum is nearest to the affected parties, since convenience is the usual test.
options.misconception: treats convenience as the test

options.text: By the wish of the government that formerly held the office, since it had the strongest interest.
options.misconception: defers to the former holder's preference

questions.explanation: The instrument of transfer, the forum it names and any later protocol together fix the answer. Assuming the old forum keeps everything, or the new one takes everything, ignores the deciding text.
questions.hint: Start with the instrument of transfer.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A ministry's account read against a local return
questions.learningObjective: State what a comparison with a local return proves and leaves open
questions.stem: Ticket 273 asks which statement best describes what a ministry account proves when a local return disagrees with it.

options.text: The ministry account proves the local return was falsified, since central records outrank district ones.
options.misconception: treats disagreement as proof of falsification

options.text: It proves a difference exists and locates the question, leaving the cause to be established.
The ministry account proves nothing, since a difference between records always means both are wrong.
options.misconception: assumes disagreement makes both records worthless

options.text: The ministry account proves the whole quarter's figures, since one official source settles the period.
options.misconception: thinks one source settles a whole period

questions.explanation: The comparison establishes that a difference exists and locates the question; it does not settle the cause. Calling it falsification or cancelling both records mistakes finding for answer.
questions.hint: Ask what the comparison establishes, not what it explains.
